United Kingdom, you have the floor.

Thank you, Chair. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of my own country, the United Kingdom, and 30 other member states of the United Nations, namely Australia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Canada, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Japan, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Luxembourg, Mexico, Moldova, Netherlands, New Zealand, North Macedonia, Norway, Palau, Romania, San Marino, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, and Uruguay. As we convene at the Commission of the Status of Women, we strongly reaffirm our unwavering determination that all women and girls have the right to live free from violence, discrimination, and oppression, to participate fully in their economies, politics, and societies. and to make the decisions which affect their lives. While we welcome the agreed conclusions on access to justice that CSW members adopted on 9 March, we still have far to go. In the 30 years since the Beijing Declaration, we have made significant progress towards gender equality around the world. The share of women in parliaments has doubled. Millions of girls have been educated. Child marriage and female genital mutilation have fallen. Maternal mortality rates have dropped, and millions more women have access to family planning. This progress has been transformative in improving the lives of millions of women and girls, as well as building our societies and our economies. Yet this progress is under threat. We are witnessing a backlash, a slowing, stalling, and even reversing of the gains we have made. Women and girls are having their autonomy restricted, legal protections weakened, and continue to face violence and discrimination. No woman or girl can access justice while they live under the threat of violence. Together, we must do more to tackle the international emergency of violence against all women and girls, because that violence is not inevitable, but preventable. As conflict and crises escalate around the world, we must work to prevent and respond to conflict-related sexual violence, support survivors, and tackle stigma. And we must tackle new forms of online violence, that cross borders, from online harassment to AI deepfakes. No society can be just where women and girls do not have a voice in the decisions that shape their lives. We must advance women's participation in politics, government, and civil society, champion women's rights organizations, and demand women's full, equal, and meaningful participation in building peace. while engaging men and boys as allies who also benefit from gender equality. Nor can a society be fair where women and girls cannot participate freely and safely in the economy. We must secure more and better jobs for women, champion women's economic leadership and participation, and support girls to access education. Women and girls cannot access justice without the right to make decisions about their own lives and their own bodies. We must ensure safe access to contraception, maternal care, and essential health services for all women and girls, including the right to safe abortion. We call on member states in every corner of the globe to resist this rollback and stand up for progress in advancing the full human rights of all women and girls, ensuring that equality is not just a list of commitments in an agreed text, but a lived reality. I thank you, Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Argentina.

Thank you very much, Madam Chair. The Argentine Republic welcomes the holding of this 70th session of the Commission on the Status of Women. While access to justice is an issue that affects both men and women, there are areas where the differential impact on women can be significant. What we have to do therefore is to reduce the gap between women and justice. For this reason, Argentina, with regard to geographic distance, has local access to justice offices, also mobile justice units and itinerant services that travel to where women are, as well as digital platforms and telephone hotlines for inquiries whose results are periodically evaluated. With respect to cultural distance, mechanisms for cultural and linguistic translation have been developed. And in some cases, indigenous jury trials and the inclusion of indigenous persons into the justice system have been implemented. With regard to when things are open, this particularly affects women. In nearly all jurisdictions of the country, we have offices that are open 24/7 for reporting violence. In general, complainants receive protective measures on the same day that the complaint is filed, all free of charge. In 2024, the Domestic Violence Office assisted 17,120 people, and 73% of complaints were received outside regular business hours. Argentina also promotes awareness of rights. A right that is unknown is a right that is not exercised. Argentina leads the movement for plain language with protocols and tools such as interpretation services, clear language information, and accessibility for women with disabilities. For women that are particularly vulnerable, an annual report on best practices regarding women's access to justice is published. The Argentine Republic, moreover, has public defenders for girls born and unborn, official defenders for women in conflict with criminal law, as well as guardians and defenders for women with restricted legal capacity, all free of charge, because we feel that vulnerability must be supported from conception until natural death. There are also systems of free legal representation, mediation, conciliation, and arbitration, all free of charge in all provinces. At the institutional level, structures have been reorganized to ensure that resources for women reach them where they are without being dispersed through bureaucratic systems. According to the latest statistics, cases have decreased by 10%. Argentina feels that justice not only needs to be accessible but also of high quality. Access to justice is ensured by having the best judges. For this reason, our country upholds the principle of merit in access to positions, promoting equal conditions between women and men. And therefore avoiding unjustified paternalism. And finally, given the many important issues that require progress in protecting women's rights, Argentina regrets that the debate has been affected by the reopening of issues already agreed upon, such as the reference to Annex IV of Beijing, which is part of the Platform for Action in its official text. This instrument constitutes a legacy that this Commission is mandated to to maintain and promote. We welcome the amendment submitted by the United States to clarify this point. Argentina reaffirms its commitment and stands ready to work in a concrete and constructive manner on the agenda of women's rights in order to build a better future. Thank you very much, Madam Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Argentina. And I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the United Arab Emirates.

Madam Chair, it is my pleasure to congratulate you on presiding over the 70th session of the CSW. I would also like to thank the UN Secretary-General for his valuable report and would like to thank UN Women for its continuous support for the work of the Committee. We would like to welcome the selection of the priority theme for this session because we believe that women and girls' access to justice is a key component of having a state based on law and advancing the rights of women and girls, especially given the challenges they face all over the world. In this framework, I would like to provide the following recommendations that we have implemented in our legal system. Firstly, we must ensure awareness among girls and women regarding their legal rights and the tools at their disposal. Therefore, we have worked to remove any barriers that prevent women from accessing the judiciary, including financial barriers. We have also established specialized units within courts and tribunals to tackle domestic abuse. Secondly, we believe that inclusive and just systems are particularly important. Therefore, we periodically review our legal systems, and these results have led to our adoption of an amended law in April of 2025, which has given women more rights. Finally, in order to have a qualitative and sustainable change, we need to have true access to data. Reliance on technology and access to proper data is essential in this regard. For example, we use the data provided in the reports in courts and police precincts in order to have better data on the issues of women and to be able to better address them. In conclusion, Madam Chair, we reaffirm our firm commitment to gender equality, and we will resume and continue our efforts to make sure that access to justice is a guaranteed right to every woman and girl. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the United Arab Emirates, and now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Sudan.

However, the current war wherein we see the Rapid Support Forces with regional support carrying out violations against all women and girls and children, including using sexual violations and sexual slavery, along with trafficking and abductions. It is very difficult to address these violations that undermine women's rights and their dignity, and this undermines our efforts as well to achieve justice. Therefore, we are working through our national bodies in order to implement a comprehensive strategy to guarantee accountability and prevent any impunity. We are taking a survivor-based approach to provide sexual and reproductive health services along with support projects and rehabilitation and reintegration projects in partnership with the civil society. We take into account that these services must be

Madam Chair, we must find methods that are compatible with the specificities of every state in order to achieve gender equality, especially in cases of armed conflict, in terms of social protection and gender equality, in order to implement the law in line with states' international obligations and also in line with national priorities. In conclusion, Madam Chair, the reform of national legal systems to make them more fair to girls and women is a matter that requires a true will and resolve, hand in hand with implementable and measurable projects. I thank the distinguished representative of Sudan, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Indonesia.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, Indonesia reaffirms its commitment to advancing gender equality and the empowerment of all women and girls, as mandated by its Constitution and national legislations. This is in line with the provisions of CEDAW and the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action, to which Indonesia subscribes. Central to this commitment is ensuring effective access to justice. Inclusive and equitable legal systems are essential to protecting women's rights, eliminating discriminatory practices, and addressing structural barriers that limit their full participation in society. In recent years, Indonesia has made steady progress in narrowing gender gaps, as reflected in improvements in both the Gender Equality Index and the Gender Development Index. Certainly, it is not without challenges. Women continue to face barriers in accessing justice for 2 main reasons. First, economic and time constraints that are often linked to the disproportionate burden of unpaid care responsibilities. And second, limited awareness of legal rights and available remedies. In this regard, allow me to highlight 3 key areas of action based on Indonesia's experience. First, strengthening legal reform and institutional measures. Access to justice has been expanded through several initiatives, including the National Action Plan on Human Rights, the introduction of electronic judicial systems to improve transparency and accessibility, and the provision of free legal aid services. Indonesia has also advanced gender-responsive adjudication through Supreme Court guidelines. Further, Indonesia has also reviewed more than 300 discriminatory regulations. Many of them have been amended or revoked. Second, strengthening protection and victim-centered services for women and children. The government has established a national reporting hotline mechanism for victims of violence, especially women and children. Meanwhile, at the grassroots level, we have encouraged local initiatives to create safe, inclusive women- and child-friendly community spaces. Third, promoting women's empowerment through integrated policies, and stronger evidence-based policymaking. Gender perspectives have been mainstreamed across sectors, including, among others, the recognition of unpaid care work through the Care Economy Roadmap, affirmative policies to strengthen women's political participation, continued improvements to data systems, and climate resilience initiatives. At the regional level, Indonesia also contributes actively through ASEAN, including in shaping the ASEAN Regional Plan of Action on the Elimination of Violence Against Women 2026-2035. Excellencies, Indonesia remains steadfast in advancing gender equality and strengthening justice systems that are accessible inclusive and responsive to the needs of women and girls. We look forward to continued collaboration.
I thank the distinguished representative of Indonesia, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Malaysia.

Thank you, Chair. Malaysia welcomes this year's priority theme and firmly believes that access to justice is a cornerstone for the realization of gender equality and the empowerment of all women and girls. Our commitment to equality is enshrined in Article 8 of Malaysia's Federal Constitution, which guarantees equality before the law and prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender. This constitutional foundation continues to guide Malaysia's efforts to strengthen legal protection and eliminate gender-based discrimination. Malaysia reaffirms its steadfast commitment to advancing women's empowerment. The National Women's Policy and the Women Development Action Plan 2025-2030 serve as the overarching frameworks guiding national efforts to advance women's empowerment across key sectors, including the economy, education, health, governance, legal protection, and access to justice. Following the enactment of the Anti-Sexual Harassment Act 2022, which established a dedicated tribunal to address sexual harassment complaints and provide victims with a clear legal pathway to seek justice, Malaysia is now developing a digital platform that will enable victims to safely submit complaints online. This initiative aims to further strengthen access to justice, particularly for women and girls in rural and underserved communities. Recognising the importance of community engagement, Malaysia has implemented grassroots initiatives such as Squad Wajah, a community-based volunteer programme that empowers individuals to act as agents of change in addressing violence against women. Through psychosocial support, awareness programmes, and community outreach, this initiative contributes to building safer communities and strengthening support networks for victims. Malaysia also recognises that strengthening access to justice requires addressing structural barriers through inclusive governance and gender-responsive policymaking. Gender mainstreaming has been institutionalized across the government through mechanisms such as gender focal points and gender focal teams across ministries and agencies. These mechanisms support evidence-based policymaking and ensure that gender perspectives are integrated into national policies, programs, and budgeting processes. Unpaid care responsibilities remain one of the key structural barriers limiting women's economic participation. Thus, Malaysia has launched the Malaysia Care Strategic Framework and Action Plan 2026-2030. By expanding accessible care services and professionalizing the care sector, the framework seeks to reduce disproportionate burden of unpaid care work on women, therefore enhancing social justice by enabling them to participate more fully in economic, social, and public life. Distinguished delegates, despite the progress achieved, much work remains. Ensuring meaningful access to justice for women and girls requires sustained political will, inclusive institutions, and strong partnerships. At all levels. Malaysia remains committed to working with Member States, the United Nations system, and all stakeholders to advance gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls. Together, we must ensure that justice systems are inclusive, responsive, and accessible, so that every woman and girl can live with dignity, exercise her rights, and contribute fully to the progress of our societies. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Malaysia, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Saint Kitts and Nevis.

Madam Chair, distinguished delegates, representatives of civil society, Saint Kitts and Nevis thanks you, Madam Chair, and commends you and the Bureau for the dedication and hard work that you bring to this Commission. Saint Kitts and Nevis notes that under your stewardship, this 70th session has risen to the moment it was called to meet. The priority theme before us, ensuring and strengthening access to justice for all women and girls, is not an abstraction for Small Island Developing States. It is a daily imperative. It is the difference between rights declared and rights delivered. Saint Kitts and Nevis is committed to closing this gap. Women and girls represent more than half of the world's population. They are not a special interest group. They are not a minority. They are the foundation upon which families, communities, and nations are built. And yet, across the globe, they continue to be denied fundamental rights. This Commission exists to change that. The theme of this 7th session is not merely timely, it is urgent, and Saint Kitts and Nevis stands fully committed to the work that it demands. Madam Chair, last year Saint Kitts and Nevis had the honour of co-facilitating the revitalization of this Commission alongside Ireland. The resolution put forward was adopted by consensus last September, and Saint Kitts and Nevis is now working to turn its words into action. Saint Kitts and Nevis has never measured its commitment by the size of its landmass. We measure it by the lives we change, and our government works assiduously every single day to ensure that the rights of our women and girls move from page into practice. We began by building the architecture. Our Gender Equality Policy and Action Plan guides gender mainstreaming across every sector of government. This is not a policy on a shelf, it is a policy in motion. We ensure that when a woman escapes violence, there is somewhere to turn. Through our partnership with the Garden of Rebirth Shelter, Women in our federation have access to counseling, legal support, and a place to heal. And we recognize that violence against women is addressed through our, our broader national approach to crime and violence as a public health issue, integrating prevention, early intervention, and rehabilitation. St. Kitts and Nevis does not wait for violence to escalate before we act. We intervene early, rehabilitate, and we protect. The women and girls, girls of Saint Kitts and Nevis are not waiting. They are leading in our civil service, our communities, our courts, and our schools. They have shelter, legal protection, and a government that sees them. Saint Kitts and Nevis leaves this session committed to carrying forward the agreed conclusions of CSW 70, not as a document to be filed, but as a mandate to be implemented. Thank you, Madam Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Saint Kitts and Nevis, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Maldives.

Thank you, Chair. All protocols observed. The Maldives reaffirms its commitment to improving the future of women and girls. This includes legal protection, representation in decision-making, economic inclusion, and many other areas so that the Maldives could invest adequately in gender equality. The Gender Equality Act in the Maldives remains the basis of our national frameworks. It promotes gender perspective in governance, It reinforced by legislation, including the Domestic Violence Prevention Act, the Sexual Offences Act, and the Prevention of Sexual Abuses and Harassment Act. Together, these instruments strengthen the protection for survivors and accountability for perpetrators. Equality before the law must translate into practice. The Maldives is improving implementation through institutional gender mainstreaming and coordination between institutions and reporting and referral mechanisms. The National Strategy for Development Gender Statistics ensures that our policies are data-driven and help us measure progress. Geographical accessibility is a necessity across our adults. The Family and Children's Services Centers provides assistance to women, children, older persons, and persons with disabilities. They work with relevant agencies, including law enforcement and the judiciary, to ensure timely prevention, protection, and support. Women's roles in governance is equally critical. Maldivian women now hold 40% of island council seats, up from 6% in 2017. Women's development committees across the islands further strengthen women's integration into local decision-making. Inclusive representation is essential. The women's— Maldivian women remain committed to improving structural barriers in politics as well as public and private sectors. The Maldives is honored to serve as a member of CSW from its next session. We look forward to continuing its work in responding to the realities and aspirations for all women and girls. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Maldives, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Greece.

Thank you, Chair. Greece remains firmly committed to the full realization of the rights of women and girls. Effective access to justice is fundamental in this regard. The key challenge today is not the absence of laws, but their consistent and effective implementation. In Greece, the legal framework on gender equality and women's access to justice is aligned with international standards. Our priority is its full operationalization. First, we have strengthened the normative basis for protection. Discrimination on the grounds of sex is explicitly prohibited, and access to judicial protection, particularly in employment, has long been secured. The ratification of the Istanbul Convention significantly reinforced our national framework for the prevention of and response to violence against women. Furthermore, our law on domestic violence recently amended in 2025, enhances criminal accountability and strengthens victim protection mechanisms. It addresses structural and emerging forms of violence, including female genital mutilation, forced marriage, and cyber harassment and technological stalking, affirming that violence, whether offline or online, must be effectively prevented and prosecuted. Second, we are addressing institutional barriers within the justice system itself. Access to justice must be survivor-centered and trauma-informed. Greece is taking steps to establish sexual violence and rape crisis centers in line with our international obligations to provide integrated and multidisciplinary support while preventing victimization. In parallel, our National Strategic Plan for Gender Equality 2026-2030 marks a strategic shift from policy design to measurable implementation with emphasis on monitoring, coordination, and accountability. Third, we are leveraging innovation to enhance protection. The nationwide expansion of the Panic Button application provides women at high risk with a discreet and immediate channel to alert law enforcement authorities. This tool complements broader prevention and early intervention strategies aimed at disrupting cycles of violence before they escalate. At the same time, we recognize that economic vulnerability can severely constrain access to justice. Financial dependence often prevents survivors from pursuing protection or legal remedies. For this reason, Greece has introduced subsidized employment programs and targeted financial support measures to promote economic autonomy and enable women to effectively exercise their rights. Excellencies, Greece remains committed to working in partnership with member states United Nations entities, and civil society to transform formal equality into lived equality and commitments into concrete results. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Greece. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the League of Arab States.

Thank you, Madam Chair. On behalf of the League of Arab States, I congratulate you on assuming the chairmanship of the 70th session of the CSW, and I congratulate the members of the Bureau too. Allow me to begin, in light of serious developments in our region, to reaffirm our condemnation of attacks against civilian facilities in several member states of the Arab League. We also condemn the ongoing Israeli occupation and its settlement practices, which have had a serious impact on women and girls. Madam Chair, access to justice is not merely about procedure. It is an absolute prerequisite for achievement of equality, and for trust in state institutions. In the Arab region, women face many challenges. These include legal barriers, social constraints, and the impacts of conflict and displacement. A lack of access to justice is an obstacle that prevents women from enjoying their rights, in particular in fragile societies. And to strengthen protection. However, there's much to be done ahead. More needs to be done to ensure legal systems that are fair. The Agenda for the Development of Arab Women in the Arab Region for the period 2023 to 2028 encompasses as well the strengthening of legislation as a priority in the Arab region. The Arab League reiterates its support to member states for the development of national legislation. The issue under review in this session calls upon us to move from commitments to the implementation of texts to achieve a real impact. This can be done only by dismantling legal and structural barriers to ensure justice for all women in all circumstances. That includes conflict and crises. The League of Arab States reiterates its commitment to working with member states and international partners in order to bolster access to justice.

On behalf of His Excellency, The Chairperson of the African Union Commission, His Excellency Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, it's an honor to address this august assembly. The African Union welcomes the convening of the 70th session of the Commission on the Status of Women under the priority theme, Ensuring and Strengthening Access to Justice for All Women and Girls, including promoting inclusive legal systems and eliminating discrimination. Discriminatory laws. This priority resonates strongly with Africa's commitment to gender equality and women's rights across our continent. Justice for women and girls is inseparable from peace, development, and human dignity. Africa has made significant progress in advancing gender equality through a robust continental normative The Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa, which is ratified by 46 out of 55 AU member states, remains one of the most progressive legal instruments globally on women's rights. Complementing this are the Solemn Declaration on Gender Equality in Africa the African Union Strategy for Gender Equality and Women's Empowerment, and Agenda 2063, which envisions an Africa where women and men fully participate in shaping the continent's development. This landmark convention represents Africa's collective determination to end one of the most pervasive human rights violations affecting our societies. To date, 8 AU member states have signed the convention, and we look forward to receiving the requisite number of ratifications to bring this important instrument into force. Excellencies, Africa's leadership in gender equality and women's empowerment extends to the global stage. In this spirit, the African Union has put forward its candidacy to host the 74th session of the Commission on the Status of Women in 2030, a historic opportunity to situate the final review of the Sustainable Development Goals within a continent that has demonstrated resilience, innovation, and leadership in advancing—

Thank you, Madam Chair. Distinguished delegates, we are all aware that as we gather at the 70th session of the Commission, it is a time of immense global upheaval. The agreed conclusions adopted last week confirm the importance of and I quote, promoting the rule of law and ensuring equal access to justice. We should celebrate the reaffirmation of these fundamental principles at a time when there is global pushback against hard-won progress on human rights and gender equality. But at the same time, we must recognize that for too many women and girls, these commitments remain distant from everyday reality. In nearly 70% of countries, women still face greater legal, financial, social, and cultural barriers to justice than men. As the only global intergovernmental organization exclusively devoted to enhancing— to advancing the rule of law to promote peace and sustainable development, IDLO's 4 decades of experience in some 100 countries confirm that turning equality from principle into practice requires strong laws, effective institutions and justice systems that work for women and girls. It also requires challenging patriarchal views and persistent social norms. Allow me to highlight 5 key actions that drive change. First, eliminating discriminatory laws and policies is the first step towards removing structural barriers to equality. Second, by building people-centered justice systems, that listen to and reflect the needs of women and girls, we don't just deliver fair outcomes, we also rebuild trust. Women's equal participation and leadership in justice institutions is also key to achieving this objective. Third, legal empowerment is essential to ensure that women are able to use the law to claim their rights. Fourth, ending gender-based violence, including cyber violence, is fundamental for women and girls to live free from fear and to contribute fully to their societies. Fifth and finally, we must invest strategically to address women's justice needs at all levels and to close the gender justice gap locally, nationally, and internationally. Empowering women through the rule of law can be transformational. It leads to more resilient families and communities, more dynamic economies, and more peaceful and inclusive societies. SDGs 5 and 16 are mutually reinforcing. Accelerating progress requires sustained political commitment, innovative approaches, adequate funding, and mobilizing broad, multi-sectoral coalitions for change. IDLO remains committed to working with all partners to strengthen the rule of law and access to justice as an essential pathway to gender equality. Thank you, Madam Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of the International Development Law Organization, and I now give the floor to the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance.

Thank you, Chair. Distinguished delegates, the theme of this year's Commission, Ensuring and Strengthening Access to Justice for All Women and Girls, speaks directly to the foundations of democratic governance. Inclusive and equitable legal systems free from discrimination are essential for enabling women to claim their rights, participate fully in public life, and hold institutions accountable. Without access to justice, gender equality and women's empowerment remain a promise rather than a lived reality. International IDEA's Global State of Democracy Indices shares that global gender equality scores have improved significantly since the adoption of the Beijing Declaration, but on— but only marginally in the past decade. Women still hold only 27.5% of parliamentary seats globally, and structural barriers including discriminatory norms, violence and harassment in politics, and unequal access to resources continue to limit women's political participation and leadership. These barriers also undermine women's access to justice. Discriminatory laws, weak accountability mechanisms, and gender-blind institutions often prevent women and girls from seeking redress and exercising their rights fully. Ensuring justice requires not only legal reform but also gender-responsive democratic institutions capable of addressing discrimination and strengthening public trust. International IDEA's work consistently shows that democracies tend to perform better on gender equality indicators than non-democratic regimes. Democratic institutions, when inclusive, transparent, and accountable, create pathways for women to influence laws, policies, and judicial systems that shape their lives. However, recent global trends provide cause for concern. Around the world, we are witnessing a backlash against gender equality and democratic values alongside shrinking civic space and rising polarization. These trends threaten the progress achieved in advancing women's rights and undermine efforts to build inclusive justice systems. Excellencies, ensuring justice for women and girls requires addressing structural barriers at every level. This includes eliminating discriminatory laws and practices, strengthening judicial and constitutional frameworks that uphold equality, and ensuring that women are meaningfully represented in institutions responsible for lawmaking, governance, and oversight. Women must not be seen merely as beneficiaries of justice systems, but as leaders and agents of change in shaping them. When women participate in decision-making, institutions become more responsive, inclusive, and legitimate. But we must not forget that achieving access to justice for all also requires addressing violence against women in politics and public life, improving data and monitoring mechanisms, and investing in institutions.

I thank the distinguished representative of the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the International Union for Conservation of Nature.

Thank you, Chair. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, as the world confronts the interlinked crisis of climate change, biodiversity loss, pollution, and rising inequality, gender equality is not only a human right, it is a prerequisite for effective and lasting environmental action. IUCN's global research shows that gender inequality continues to limit the resilience of communities, the sustainability of ecosystems, and the success of environmental policy. At the same time, the evidence is clear: when women and girls have equal rights, access, voice, and leadership, environmental outcomes improve and climate ambition rises. The theme of the 70th CSW is particularly relevant to IUCN's work on addressing gender-based violence linked to the environment and to access and control over natural resources, as well as their work to protect and defend women environmental rights defenders. IUCN's research has documented the connections between environmental pressures, resource scarcity, and increased risk of gender-based violence. We know that violence is used as a systemic tool of control to reinforce power imbalances, and at times violently discouraging or stopping women from speaking out for their rights. Environmental action must include mitigation, prevention, and response measures, ensuring that women and girls can benefit from conservation efforts and participate, participate safely and meaningfully. Even as major environmental frameworks acknowledge the importance of environmental human rights defenders, their safety continues to deteriorate. Since the adoption of the Paris Agreement in 2015, more than 1,500 defenders have been murdered, an approximate of one every other day. In '23 alone, nearly half of those killed were Indigenous leaders, and 12% were women. This reflects a deeply rooted pattern of gendered and racialized violence, which is not only a matter of environmental justice, it's a human rights crisis. As a rights-based union, IUCN is committed to strengthening protections and advancing access to justice for women and women environmental human rights defenders. We are supporting community-led efforts to address, mitigate, and respond to gender-based violence in the context of environmental conservation and the protection of Indigenous women environmental human rights defenders. We call on member states to take urgent and coordinated action, including facilitating access and meaningful participation in environmental decision-making processes and recognizing the vital role that women and Indigenous leaders play in their communities. Achieving gender equality is not separate from environmental ambition. It is—

Thank you, Madam Chair. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, access to justice is a core human right and affirmation of one's dignity. Yet many women and girls still struggle to access justice for gender-based crimes. When perpetrators enjoy impunity, this sends a devastating message that women and girls' suffering can be dismissed, their rights disregarded, and their dignity undermined. As the world's largest police organization, Interpol is committed to fight impunity and strengthening enforcement, particularly in addressing gender-based violence. Allow me to highlight 3 ways we are doing so. First, we help global authorities bring perpetrators of gender-based crimes to justice. Our Red Notices can alert law enforcement about fugitives wanted for crimes against women and girls, including sexual violence, bodily injury, and murder. These are shared with all our member countries, ensuring that crossing borders does not mean escaping accountability. Her name was Eva Maria Palmer, and after 20 years, her family was finally given closure. Third, we strive— we drive structural change within the criminal justice system by uplifting women in law enforcement. Women continue to be underrepresented in law enforcement leadership or confined to administrative roles, partly due to the unequal access to training opportunities. Accordingly, Interpol is investing in training and fellowship programs for female police officers, including through Project Momentum MENA, which has trained over 220 officials since 2024. Excellencies, when half of the world's population faces barriers in accessing justice, this is a grave injustice that affects us all. Interpol remains committed to uniting law enforcement to deliver justice for women and girls so that their dignity is respected, protected, and defended under the law. I thank you.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Excellencies, distinguished guests, it is an honor to address this distinguished gathering at the 70th session of the Commission on the Status of Women at a time when the international community must strengthen its resolve to ensure that women's contributions and rights are fully recognized and supported. This year, we celebrate the International Year of the Woman Farmer 2026, which provides great opportunity to elevate the visibility, leadership, and contributions of women farmers in agri-food systems, while advancing policies and investments that empower all women working in these systems. It is also an opportunity to promote greater synergies among international initiatives supporting women farmers. Women farmers are indispensable actors in agrifood systems, making up around 40% of the global agrifood force. Yet their contributions remain undervalued and are constrained by persistent gender inequalities. Across contexts, women have less secure access to and control over lands, as well as finance, fewer opportunities for education and extension services, and limited participation in decision-making spaces. Spaces that shape agricultural policies and rural development pathways. The International Year of the Woman Farmer aims to raise awareness about these challenges and to catalyze policy reforms, investments, and collective action that empower women farmers and strengthen food security, nutrition, economic security, climate resilience, and rural livelihoods. Gender equality and the empowerment of women farmers are integral to to FAO's mandates. Our latest evidence, including the Status of Women in Agrifood Systems, the Unjust Climate, and the Status of Youth in Agrifood Systems reports, underscores the magnitude of structural gender disparities in agrifood systems and their adverse effects on productivity, incomes, and resilience. FAO estimates that across agrifood systems, women earn just 78 cents for every dollar earned by men, and women farmers, who often cultivate smaller plots, still face a 24% productivity gap even when managing farms of the same size. But FAO analysis also points to clear opportunities. When women farmers have equal access to land, technologies, finance, and market, productivity rises. hunger falls, and rural economies become more robust. FAO underscores that closing the gender gaps in farm productivity and wages could raise global gross domestic product by $1 trillion and reduce food insecurity for 45 million people. FAO continues to work closely with other UN agencies.

Distinguished delegates, colleagues, access to justice for women and girls in all their diversity resonates with WHO's mandate. Without health systems working to advance justice for women and girls, achieving their right to the highest attainable standard of health will remain unfulfilled. When women and girls cannot claim their health-related rights or obtain remedies when violations occur, justice is denied and inequities deepen. 30 years after the Beijing Declaration, important gains have been made. Births among adolescent girls have declined, more women have their contraception needs met with modern methods, and maternal mortality has fallen. Yet injustices persist. Structural barriers, including discriminatory laws, policies, and practices, continue to prevent women and girls from accessing affordable, acceptable, and quality healthcare. These injustices continue to determine who is heard, who is protected, and who is left behind. Women still face maternal health risks, especially in conflict-affected and institutionally fragile contexts, while climate change, household air pollution, and humanitarian crises threaten their health. Adolescent girls account for a disproportionate share of new HIV infections. Women who have experienced intimate partner violence or sexual violence particularly vulnerable to developing mental health conditions. Health systems are often the primary institutions with which women and girls engage, including when seeking help after violence. Justice for women and girls means health systems informed by sex-disaggregated data that represents everyone. It means taking action to advance sexual and reproductive health and rights. It means ensuring access to information and services that enable bodily autonomy and informed decisions about when and where to seek appropriate healthcare, including for fertility and contraception. It means receiving non-discriminatory and quality healthcare. Justice means ending all forms of violence against against women and girls and access to safe accountability mechanisms when health rights are violated. Justice also means redressing gender inequalities in the health workforce and recognizing that women constitute 67% of the health workforce. WHO reaffirms our commitment to supporting member states in undertaking meaningful reforms to ensure rights based and gender-responsive health systems.

Thank you very much, Chairperson. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, Zambia congratulates you and the Bureau on your leadership of the 70th session of the Commission on the Status of Women, and we have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the Government of the Republic of Zambia. Zambia reaffirms its strong commitment to the full implementation of the Beijing Declaration and Platform of Action, CEDAW, and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, particularly Goals 5 and 16 on gender equality, justice, and strong institutions. Distinguished delegates, in line with this year's priority theme, Zambia has undertaken significant legislative, policy, and programmatic reforms to strengthen access to justice for women and girls. Victim-centered and trauma-informed systems have been established, including specialized courts and coordinated police prosecution and medical services, with the state covering the cost accessing justice. A robust legal framework supports these efforts, including the Penal Code, the Anti-Gender-Based Violence Act, and the Gender Equality and Equality Act. Zambia has also outlawed child marriage through the Children's Code Act and the Marriage Amendment Act. Further, innovative approaches have been expanded for survivor support, including using confiscated assets to establish shelters for survivors and establishing remote evidence centers to enable victims to testify safely outside physical courtrooms. Zambia has also bold— taken bold constitutional steps to strengthen inclusive governance. The Constitution Amendment Act Number 13 of 2025 introduces a mixed-member proportional representation system reserving seats for women, youth, and persons with disabilities aimed at significantly increasing women's representation in Parliament. These reforms build on recent milestones, including the appointment of women to the offices of Vice President, Speaker of the National Assembly, and Minister of Justice. As Africa Union champion on ending child marriage, Zambia continues to prioritize girls' education through free education policy, strengthened police school entry guidelines, and school feeding programs. These efforts have contributed to a decline in child marriage from 29% in 2018 to 23.9% in 2024. Government is also expanding health and social protection services, strengthening maternal health facilities, and investing in community development through the Constituency Development Fund, which supports school infrastructure, health services, and women-led initiatives. Your Excellencies, while progress is evident, challenges remain, including harmful social norms, unequal access to productive resources, women's underrepresentation in elective positions, and the persistent impact of gender-based violence. Zambia recognizes that accelerating progress requires strong partnerships and increased financing for gender equality and including gender-responsive plans— planning, greater investment in girls' education, and expanded economic opportunities for women. In conclusion, Zambia remains firmly committed to ensuring that every woman girl enjoys equal rights, opportunities, and protection under the law. When women and girls thrive, families prosper, communities grow stronger, and the nation develops sustainably. Zambia stands ready to work with all member states, development partners, civil society, the private sector, and other stakeholders to turn the promises of the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action into lived realities for women and girls everywhere. I thank you.

Thank you, Chair. Your Excellencies, distinguished delegates, dear partners, the International Telecommunication Union, United Nations Specialized Agency for Digital Technology, is pleased to contribute to discussion at the 70th session of the Commission on the Status of Women, and I'm honored to deliver this statement today. This year's review theme on women's full and effective participation and decision-making in public life is particularly timely because today participation in public life increasingly happens in digital spaces. From civic engagement to access to services and information, digital technologies are now shaping how women participate, express their voices, and influence decisions. But participation in the digital age is not guaranteed. Despite progress, the gender digital divide remains significant. Globally, 77% of men use the internet compared to 71% of women, representing around 280 million fewer women online. This gap is not only about connectivity. It's about access to opportunity, to information, and to meaningful participation in public life. And when participation is limited, whether due to lack of access, skills, or safety, women's ability to engage, to be heard, and to seek redress and accountability is also affected in practice. At ITU, our work focuses on addressing these barriers through 3 key areas: expanding meaningful connectivity, strengthening digital skills and pathways, and promoting women leadership in the digital sector. We support member states in integrating gender equality into digital policies, strengthening women's participation in ICT governance, and ensuring that digital transformation delivers inclusive outcomes. We also work through global partnerships, such as the EQUALS Global Partnership on Gender Equality in the Digital Age, and through concrete initiatives that equip women and girls with the skills, confidence, and opportunity to engage fully in the digital age. We welcome the strengthened recognition of gender equality within global digital framework. The World Summit on Information Society+20 outcome document that was adopted by consensus in December 2025 reinforced the importance of inclusive digital transformation and calls for the full and equal meaningful participation of women and girls in the information society. To further advance work in this area, ITU has established a dedicated Gender and Youth Office reporting directly to the Secretary-General to strengthen and institutionalize our efforts across the organization. Distinguished delegates, as public life becomes increasingly digital, ensuring inclusion, safety, and equal opportunity in these spaces is essential.

Thank you, Chairperson. More than 21 million women and girls live with HIV worldwide, accounting for 53% of all people living with HIV. Even where the protection— protective laws exist, justice systems remain inaccessible for many women and girls living with or at risk of HIV. Community-led organizations, including those led by women, play a critical role by providing legal aid as well as HIV prevention, treatment, and support services more generally. However, the abrupt cuts in HIV funding since early 2025 have particularly affected community-led programs. More than 60% of women-led HIV organizations have lost funding and been forced to suspend vital services. Against this background, the CSW resolution on women, the girl child, and HIV/AIDS is ever more important. UNAIDS commends the continued leadership of the Southern African Development Community, SADC, on this issue. We welcome the draft resolution tabled by South Africa on behalf of the SADC and call on Member States to adopt it by consensus as usual. Chairperson, Remarkable progress has been made against AIDS, but it is not over. The 2025 targets expired, most of which have not been achieved. The 2026 High-Level Meeting on HIV/AIDS will be a critical opportunity to bring together leaders from governments, UN, civil society, and private sector to renew the political and financial commitment to end AIDS by 2030 and to adopt an ambitious political declaration that will set new targets to guide the HIV response towards that goal. Protecting the rights, health, and well-being of all women and girls, including those living with, at risk of, or affected by HIV, investing in their empowerment and inclusion in decision-making in all spheres, must be at the center of the discussions at the high-level meeting and its outcomes. We call on all stakeholders to participate at the meeting at the highest possible level and to actively contribute to its success. Thank you.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Let me begin with something simple. If we are serious about advancing the status of women, we cannot retire women from the agenda of this Commission at age 60. It is therefore encouraging that this session included a ministerial panel on this issue last week. And on behalf of the United Nations Interagency Group on Ageing, let me say clearly, this attention by the Commission is welcome, it is timely, and frankly, it is long overdue. The reality is this: older women are not a marginal group. They're one of the fastest-growing segments of the female population, yet so often, too often, absent in discussions on women's advancement. Not absent in reality, mind you, but absent in framing, absent in data narratives, and absent in policy design. This disconnect should give us pause. It raises an uncomfortable question: why do discussions on the status of women so often focus on the beginning and the middle of the course of life, yet grow quieter in later life? Recognizing this is not about setting age groups in opposition. It is about correcting blind spots, because when age is not explicitly considered, it is rarely implicitly addressed. It is perhaps no surprise that applying an age lens requires such determination when we recall that age was not explicitly articulated in the founding blueprint of the United Nations 80 years ago. From the perspective of the 32 members of the UN Interagency Group on Aging, 3 priorities are clear. First, keep older women firmly and consistently on the agenda in this Commission's discussions. Second, ensure that the Commission's outcomes explicitly reflect the realities of women in later life. And third, create intentional space for older women themselves to participate in shaping the discussions and priorities that affect their lives. And to the girls, the young women, and adult women here, like myself and you, Madam Chair, we do not lose space when older women gain it. We gain allies— older women that advocate not only for themselves, but also for our future. Chair, we hope this session marks not a temporary spotlight on older women, but a turning point for their inclusion in the Commission's future work, including forthcoming priority themes. And as part of this collective effort, I invite you to draw on the Interagency Group on Ageing's common messages. And on behalf of the group, we stand ready to support member states in advancing this agenda. I thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the International Labour Organization.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Ensuring and strengthening access to justice for all women is essential to advancing social justice, and there can be no social justice without women's rights and gender equality in the world of work. Access to justice means that women workers are able not only to know their rights, but also to claim them and obtain effective remedies when those rights are violated. This requires inclusive and equitable legal systems, as well as effective labour dispute prevention and resolution mechanisms. In the world of work, these mechanisms include workplace grievance procedures, labor inspection systems, mediation and conciliation services, as well as labor courts and tribunals, and importantly, freedom of association and the right to organize. When they function effectively, they allow workers and employers to address grievances, enforce labor rights, and resolve disputes fairly and efficiently, ensuring that labor rights are translated into protection in practice. Access to justice in the world of work is strongly linked to freedom of association, the right to organize, and collective bargaining. These fundamental labor rights support democracy at work, enabling the representation and collective voice of workers to both prevent and address violations of their rights. Despite progress, many women today continue to face structural barriers in accessing justice. Legal frameworks may not fully protect women's— women workers' rights, and sectors where women are overrepresented, such as domestic work and agricultural work, may remain outside the scope of labor law protections. Women may also face practical and social barriers, including limited access to information about their rights affordable legal assistance, or collective representation. Discriminatory norms, fear of retaliation, economic dependency, and social stigma may further discourage women from seeking justice. ILO Convention No. 190 on Violence and Harassment in the World of Work, now ratified by 54 countries, provides a comprehensive roadmap for access to justice in the world of work. It provides coverage for all involved in the world of work, whether in the informal or formal economy, rural or urban areas, whether a job seeker, intern, or apprentice. It calls for accessible, safe, and gender-responsive reporting and dispute resolution mechanisms, protection against retaliation, training for employers, workers, and relevant authorities, and access to remedies and support services for victims. Through its normative framework, technical cooperation, knowledge development, and tripartite structure, the ILO works to ensure that women workers can effectively access justice, claim their rights, and fully participate in the world of work. I thank you.

Madam Chair, the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights welcomes the timely focus this year's Commission on Access to Justice and the adoption of the agreed conclusions. We also welcome the special focus placed on older women this year, long overdue, as my colleagues just said. Ensuring women's access to justice is not only a legal obligation, it is a foundation for equality, dignity, and the full realization of all human rights. International human rights law The Beijing Declaration and Platform of Action, 2030 Agenda, and Security Council Resolution 1325 all make clear that justice systems must work for women and girls. Access to justice and the right to an effective remedy are inseparable from the right to equality in both private and public life. But for this to be real, Justice systems must be independent, impartial, adequately funded, and grounded in the rule of law. They must guarantee due process and be guided by international human rights standards. Justice is also a powerful instrument against poverty and discrimination. It enables women to claim their rights, including economic and social rights, the recognition of unpaid care work, to seek alimony from— and social protections, and to challenge sexual harassment, unfair labor practices, and discriminatory laws and norms. Encouragingly, between 2019 and 2024, nearly 100 positive legal reforms were adopted worldwide to eliminate discrimination and strengthen gender equality frameworks. Yet laws alone are not enough. Women of all ages, including young girls and older women, need accessible, gender- and age-sensitive justice across all courts and administrative bodies. Legal aid, especially for women in low-income or vulnerable situations, is essential to ensure justice is truly universal. Not a privilege only for those who can afford it. Parity in the judiciary, the sustained capacity building on women's rights for judges, prosecutors, legal professionals, and law enforcement are also vital. Tackling gender stereotypes within justice systems remains a persistent challenge that demands renewed commitment from member states. OSCE will continue to support states through technical assistance and by working closely with women's organizations, women's human rights defenders, to ensure that every woman and girl can access justice without discrimination. Thank you.
