Thank you, Madam Chair. Action by Churches Together, ACT Alliance, is a faith-based, rights-based coalition with over 153 members working in 125 countries. Access to justice is not only a legal matter, it is a moral imperative and a cornerstone of gender equality. Around the world, millions of women and girls continue to face discriminatory laws, patriarchal norms, and legal systems that are inaccessible, be unsafe. Reforming legislation is essential, but laws alone cannot transform societies when the social norms beneath them remain unchanged. As faith-based actors, who are rooted in our communities. We witness how faith leaders can either reinforce harmful practices or become powerful allies in dismantling them. When faith-based leaders act against gender-based discrimination, challenge harmful norms, and affirm human rights, we can push forward on the road to gender equality. Theological framework that uphold human rights, equality, and bodily autonomy can serve as profound tool for justice reform, helping to confront violence, expand access to sexual reproductive health and rights, and advance the rights of women and girls in all their diversities. We call on member states to reform discriminatory family and personal status laws, including those rooted in religious systems, so that all women have equal rights, including in marriage, inheritance, and economic life. Promote economic justice, ensuring women equal access to land, credit, decent work, and microeconomic policies that prioritize equality. Guarantee survivor-centered, trauma-informed responses to all forms of violence. Violence, develop gender transformative transitional justice mechanism in fragile and conflict-affected setting, fully implement regional commitments to sexual and reproductive health and rights such as the Maputo Protocol. We invite for a reflection on the people not in the room today. To advance justice, CSW itself must model justice. Today, shrinking civil spaces, visa denials, and unequal access prevent grassroots feminists, faith-based peacebuilders, and human rights defenders from participating in the very forum meant to elevate their voice. CSW 70 must not become a platform of exclusion. We urge member states and UN leadership to uphold.

I thank the distinguished representative of the ACT Alliance, Action by Churches Together, and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the United Nations Office for Project Services.

Thank you, Madam Chair. UNOPS is honored to participate in this forum and to share how, in partnership with governments and other stakeholders, we help address the challenges women face worldwide, particularly in fragile and remote contexts. As the operational arm of the United Nations working in infrastructure procurement and project services, UNOPS focuses on turning commitments into action. Our work helps translate policies into practical solutions that expand women's access to services, opportunities, and decision-making in their communities. UNOPS integrates gender-responsive approaches in all its projects and operations. In infrastructure projects, that— this includes setting targets for women's participation in construction and engineering roles while ensuring that health facilities, schools, and water systems are designed with gender-sensitive features that improve access to education, health, and essential services. Earlier this month, In the lead-up to International Women's Day, UNOPS launched its gender-responsive procurement guidelines. Women remain largely excluded from one of the world's largest economic opportunities, public procurement. Of the approximately $11 trillion spent globally each year by governments and international organizations, less than 1% is awarded to women-owned businesses. By making procurement more inclusive and equitable, UNOPS aims to open doors for women entrepreneurs and promote fair competition in the marketplace. UNOPS also supports women's livelihood and economic empowerment. In countries such as Afghanistan and Myanmar, we implement cash-for-work projects, skills training, and support for women-led small businesses, enabling women to generate income and participate more fully in local economies. Agile fee-for-service business model allows us to respond quickly in fragile and conflict-affected settings, ensuring support reaches those who face the greatest barriers. In Ukraine, for example, UNOPS is rebuilding bridges, repairing schools and homes, and restoring essential infrastructure while providing cash for work activities that engage women directly in community recovery. Across these operations, UNOPS addresses both immediate humanitarian needs and long-term empowerment, placing women at the center of recovery and sustainable development efforts. We measure success in large part by the extent to which women can access infrastructure that meets their needs, participate in community decision-making, and benefit from education, health, and economic opportunities. Madam Chair, UNOPS remains committed to forging partnerships and advancing projects that turn policies into real-world impact for women and girls, bridging the implementation gap and supporting sustainable, inclusive development fully aligned with the United Nations values on women's empowerment and gender equality. I have—

I thank the distinguished representative of the United Nations Office for Project Services and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Associação de Cauães Inga Comando. Forgive my poor Portuguese abilities.

Thank you. Distinguished Chair, delegates, and fellow activists, we stand before this Commission as part of a global collective of youth leaders and adolescents whose voices were mobilized through consultations across the globe. This process reflects a extensive political mandate shaped by live realities across regions and generations. Our message is clear: access to justice must be understood as a structural priority. Transforming patriarchal masculinities is essential to dismantle legal systems that shield perpetrators. Rigid gender norms and male supremacy ideology within justice institutions foster impunity and block rights of women and girls. We therefore advocate for gender transformative justice that addresses root causes of discrimination and promotes institutional cultures grounded in equality, accountability, and prevention. These are some of the reasons why the CSW70 Global Youth and Adolescent Recommendations exist. Our document is a product of the youth consultations organized by youth activists in more than 70 countries and that mobilized more than 23,000 young leaders worldwide, generating a shared political vision for structural change. In our recommendations, we remind the Commission that there is no gender justice without climate justice. For young women in the Global South, the climate crisis is a legal crisis. We call on justice systems to recognize the displacement due to extreme weather events, address the climate debt owed to the future generations and ensure the protection of environmental defenders who continue to face criminalization for safeguarding our shared home. Therefore, we demand action. Transform the laws, fund the movements, and deliver justice now. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Associação de Jovens em Garimpo, and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Association for the Defense of the Rights of Azerbaijani Women in Iran.

Thank you. Madam Chair, Excellencies, Association for the Defense of Human Rights of Azerbaijanis in Iran welcomes this important dialogue and stresses that access to justice for all women and girls cannot be realized without addressing the compounded barriers faced by those who experience discrimination on the basis of gender, language, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status. In Iran, all women face systemic discrimination embedded in laws, policies, and practices that restrict equality, bodily autonomy, participation, and meaningful access to justice. However, Azerbaijani women and girls, along with other ethnically and linguistically marginalized women and girls, face additional and intersecting forms of exclusion that further weakens their access to rights remedies and protection. One of the most serious structural barriers is the denial of mother language education. When Azerbaijani girls are deprived of education in their own language, the consequences extend far beyond the learning outcomes. The denial weakens literacy, reduces legal awareness, limits access to information and undermines confidence in institutions and formal processes. Over time, this creates a cycle in which women and girls are less able to understand their rights, seek remedies, and navigate legal systems and participate fully in civic and social life. The barriers have concrete and harmful consequences. Educational exclusion contributes to lower socioeconomic status and leaves women and girls more vulnerable to child and underage marriage, exploiting a coercive or self-serving interpretation of laws and religious norms. It also weakens access to legal protection, support systems, and reporting mechanisms that reduces participation in social networks and public decision-making spaces. For young women and girls in particular, linguistic and educational exclusion often becomes a lifelong barrier to justice. Besides illiteracy, the digital dimension of these effects must also be recognized, which deprive the non-Persian-speaking women and girls of any education on women's health issues and their bodily autonomy. And yet women in Iran have been at the forefront of recent uprising and demanding dignity and equality for freedom. This includes the women from Azerbaijan and other marginalized communities whose courage must be met with protection and representation and justice. We urge the United Nations members states and relevant international mechanisms and explicitly address the denial of mother language education and related structural discrimination in Iran.

I thank the distinguished representative of the Association for the Defense of the Rights of Azerbaijani Women in Iran and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Best Practices Policy Project.

Thank you for this opportunity. My name is Nijay Lurie, and I'm a representative of the Best Practices Policy Project. We are a U.S.-based sex worker and trans-led organization focused on holding the United States accountable for human rights abuses. My message is a simple one: sex worker rights are human rights. By that, not only do I mean that those in the sex trades must be recognized as fully realized rights holders, but it also must be recognized that violations of our rights are intrinsically linked to the violation of the rights of transgender, the disabled, migrants, Black, Indigenous, and people of color. Laws that criminalize us today are the frameworks used to criminalize other populations tomorrow. There will be no justice for women and girls LGBTQIA+ people without abolishing the carceral systems that criminalize their poverty and survival. Furthermore, the conflation of sex work with trafficking harms all parties. Sex workers seek justice against discriminatory laws that want to erase us from public life. We were excluded from pandemic relief, Denied access to banking and online platforms simply for being identified as sex workers. These moralistic restrictions lay the legal foundation to deny sexual freedom and economic freedom to all minority groups. As an activist in the United States, we are concerned about the impact of U.S. policies globally. Aid and funding should be aligned with furthering human rights and not moralistic punishment. Instead of focusing on harm reduction, HIV/AIDS care, health, and housing, U.S. policy focuses on increasing stigma and imprisonment. The U.S. accepted UPR Recommendation 86 in 2010, which demanded the reduction of stigma and access to public services for sex worker transgender, and people of color, yet the criminalization, surveillance, and deplatforming of sex workers has only increased since then. There has been a shocking increase in proposed anti-LGBTQIA+ and age verification bills that seek to legislate populations out of public life. We must stand up for the humanity and dignity of all, and no nation be able to impose its narrow definitions of gender or labor rights on others. All nations should be held accountable equally. The rapid erosion of rights has to be confronted boldly and loudly. Sex worker rights are human rights.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Best Practices Policy Project I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Campaign Life Coalition.

Thank you, Chair. Campaign Life Coalition is a national nonprofit organization in Canada dedicated to protecting human life from conception to natural death and strengthening the natural family. As the Commission considers how to ensure and strengthen access to justice for women and girls, we must begin with a fundamental principle. Justice must be rooted in respect for the inherent dignity and equal worth of every human being. Without the right to life, all other rights become meaningless. Yet today, millions of the most vulnerable human beings are denied the most basic right. Abortion deliberately ends the life of an innocent human being. It kills a child in the womb. No legal system can truly claim to be inclusive or equitable while allowing the intentional killing of one class of human beings. A just society must protect the weak, not exclude them. At the same time, many women are told that abortion is their only solution when facing difficult circumstances. This is not justice. Women deserve better than a system that offers them the death of their own child as the answer to poverty, fear, or lack of support. Real justice means ensuring that women receive actual accurate information, compassionate care, and genuine alternatives. Around the world, thousands of organizations provide mothers with practical support such as prenatal and postnatal care, financial assistance, baby supplies, as well as counseling and healing for those who have experienced abortion. These life-affirming solutions truly empower women without ending the life of their child. However, some governments have adopted laws that silence those who offer this help. So-called bubble zones around abortion facilities criminalize peaceful conversations words of encouragement, and offers of assistance to pregnant women. These laws do not expand justice; they restrict it by silencing voices that seek to protect both mother and child. We must also address the growing problem of ideological colonization. Too often, international aid and development assistance are conditioned on the adoption of abortion policies that contradict the cultural and legal traditions of many nations. Maternal mortality is a serious concern, but killing children is not the solution. The real solution includes improving maternal healthcare, trained medical professionals, strengthening legal protections for mothers and their children, and building stronger support systems for families. True justice demands that every human life be protected. It demands that women be supported, not pressured, and it demands that nations be respected in their efforts to defend both mothers and their children. Campaign Life Coalition therefore calls on the Commission to reject policies that promote abortion, silence pro-life voices, or pressure nations to abandon their commitment to the right to life. Instead, let us recommit to building legal systems that defend human dignity at every stage of life and provide real support so that mothers, fathers, and their children can flourish. Thank you.
I, I thank the distinguished representative of the Campaign Life Coalition and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of CFAM Inc.

Thank you, Madam Chair. There can be no true justice unless it extends to all people, men and women, boys and girls, throughout their entire lives, including both before and after birth. That abortion is not a subject of human rights law is the long-standing UN consensus reached at the 1994 International Conference on Population and Development. The legal status of abortion is solely for individual countries to determine. It is not the place of the UN agencies or the experts tasked with ensuring that consensually agreed and duly ratified human rights treaties are implemented to create new rights. International human rights law requires that women are able to enjoy all their human rights, including the right to effective remedies on a basis of equality with men. This— they must not be excluded from justice on the basis of their sex, nor does their sex entitle them to rights not shared by men. Most countries impose some limits or criminal penalties on the practice of abortion, and this applies to any person who provides an abortion regardless of their sex. Women's access to justice cannot be seen as dependent on their right to take the lives of their unborn children with impunity. This is a blatant and intentional misreading of binding international law. As the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights states, every human being has the inherent right to life. This right shall be protected by law. No one shall be arbitrarily deprived of his life. The unborn child is a human being. This is not merely a legal determination. It is a matter of basic biology. Abortion denies the child in the womb the right to life, which is the foundation upon which all rights rest, including the right to effective remedies. Finally, the United Nations exists to be a place where debates can occur on important issues across differences. Issues of gender and sexuality remain areas of intense contestation among both governments and members of civil society. It is therefore problematic for UN officials to characterize one side in a political debate as a backlash or pushback for contesting proposals that have never earned approval by consensus. The governments of the world have negotiated, debated, and agreed to a lengthy list of goals that remain unfinished, such as ending preventable maternal and child mortality, and ensuring access to food, peace, justice, and security for all. If we are to speak of progress, then let us measure it by fulfilling what has already been promised, not by trying to force through what has not and will not be agreed. Thank you.
We thank the distinguished representative of CFAM-INC and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Christian Council International.

Thank you, Chair, for this opportunity to speak. I deliver this statement on behalf of Christian Council International. While many organizations and member states regard the outcome document as a positive step for the advancement of women and girls, we wish to express our concern regarding the process that led to its adoption. From the start of negotiations on the agreed conclusions, civil society organizations could not participate in a meaningful way. Instead of conducting the primary negotiations during the session itself, the Commission was presented with a finalized text on the first day of the session for consideration. Transparency, accountability, and constructive involvement by civil society organizations in the drafting of the text were disregarded, to say the least. Noteworthy in this regard is also the fact that member states were affected by this method of work, as the latest draft of the text was circulated less than 24 hours prior to its adoption. This was also on a day many Christians consider a day of rest and sanctification. This limited their ability to review, consult, and contribute in good faith. As a young person who is interested in the processes and procedures United Nations, I find these actions deeply troubling. The spirit in which these actions were carried out conveyed not openness, but a willingness to silence member states and the values they represent. The adopted text calls upon member states to engage with civil society to ensure equity and transparency. Yet the working methods of this session stand in clear tension with that commitment. Article 71 of the Charter of the United Nations recognizes the consultative role of the non-governmental organizations in the work of the United Nations, and Resolution 1996-6 emphasizes broad-based participation, information sharing, and meaningful NGOs engagement. Action-oriented conclusions arise from dialogue, panel discussions, and the participation of NGOs, not from from closed processes. By avoiding critical reflection and disregarding numerous calls by CSOs in several member states, the Commission has weakened its credibility. The failure to reach consensus on the outcome document suggests that many distinguished members of the Commission are reluctant to critically examine current trends concerning women's rights. For example, there has been a failure to acknowledge the biological realities that define a woman. A disregard for the family unit and the invaluable role that millions of mothers play in the upbringing of their children, and a tendency to promote reproductive rights in a way that violate the human dignity of the unborn child.

Thank you, Excellencies, distinguished guests. Concepts of Truth provides counseling for women and girls in sexual and maternal health. Based on our experience with thousands of clients and an ever-increasing amount of scientific research, we take issue with what the UN calls sexual and reproductive healthcare Namely abortion. When it comes to abortion, women simply don't make informed decisions. They don't make informed decisions because the truth is globally suppressed. A lot about abortion harms is not widely known, and I'm referring today to what the UN calls legal and safe abortions. Women aren't told how much abortion hurts them. Because reporting is mostly not required. In the U.S., only 27 states even report abortion complications. For chemical abortions, the only complication that U.S. providers are required to report is death. Most women don't die from abortion, but they do suffer many other harms. Outside the U.S., harms from abortion are greatly underreported. In many European countries, for example, there's no legal requirement for a private clinic to report surgical complications unless the patient dies. Again, many women suffer terrible harms short of death. We have the science about these harms. It's just not provided to the women and girls who need it most. Thousands of peer-reviewed studies show that women who abort have Significant increased risk of psychiatric disorders, substance abuse, suicide, and other harms. Nearly every day, our international crisis helpline gets calls from these post-abortive women, which confirms these harms. Women and girls also aren't told about the harms of gender-affirming care. There's no evidence that gender-affirming treatments provide any health benefits to minors with gender dysphoria. There's no evidence they curtail suicide. Actually, these treatments harm youth, mostly girls. They cause infertility, sexual dysfunction, psychiatric disorders, and many more harms— harms that are often irreversible. Most youth receive these treatments after little or no psychological counseling and often without knowledge of their parents. Education programs and policies that encourage youth to change their biological sex are harmful and dangerous. That's why some countries have banned gender-affirming care treatments for youth altogether. If member states and UN agencies really want to protect women and girls, they must provide them with the truth they're entitled to so they can get the justice they deserve. Thank you.
We thank the distinguished representative of the Concepts of Truth Inc. And now the the floor to the distinguished representative of the Congregations of Saint Joseph. You have the floor.

The statement is delivered on behalf of the NGO Mining Working Group. The rapid exploitation of natural resources has devastated the environment and adversely impacted human rights, especially those of women and girls. We see similar issues repeated globally in areas affected by extractives. Women must walk longer distances to access clean water, contend with dust-covered crops, and risk subjection to gender-based violence. Land dispossession, forced eviction, and forced labor undermine women's capacity to provide for themselves and their families. Women environmental and human rights defenders confronting mining activity face retaliation, intimidation, sexual harassment, and even rape and death. Indeed, the rapacious extraction of natural resources throughout colonial history has long violated human rights, the right to self-determination, and the rule of law. For example, the ICJ's 2024 advisory opinion on the illegality of Israel's occupation underscored Israel's unlawful appropriation of natural resources. States have taken no substantive action in regard to their obligations as outlined in the opinion and subsequent General Assembly resolution. Instead, the genocide and ethnic cleansing continue. A precedent of impunity is an unacceptable norm. We see this lack of accountability also in regard to heightened sexual and gender-based violence in extractive communities. The presence of non-local miners and security forces is linked with frequent experiences of sexual violence among women and girls living nearby, a common experience in the Amazon region of Brazil. Standing with women and girls affected by extractivism everywhere, the NGO Mining Working Group calls on States to ensure the regulation of businesses, including by instituting mandatory human rights and environmental due diligence and related measures that hold corporations to account. States should further promote women and Indigenous representation in decision-making processes and ensure the right to free, prior, and informed consent. They should safeguard women and girls in extractive communities by effectively addressing the differentiated risks.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Congregation of Saint Joseph and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Coptic Orphans Support Association.

Chair, Excellencies, and distinguished delegates, on behalf of Coptic Orphans, allow me to illustrate the importance of the grassroots work that makes the efforts that we've talked about in this room possible and realizes the institutional policies that we've discussed during this forum. Imagine a girl growing up in Sharona, a small rural village along the Nile in Egypt. The nearest school is across the river, accessible only by boat. Unable to reach the school, she drops out at 11 years old like most girls in her village. She has no literacy skills. As the years pass, her dependence on others grows and her choices narrow. In her town, most girls are marriage by— married by 18. Her mother's experience echoes this path, married at 14, her first child at 15. and widowed by 26. It is this girl's inevitable fate. This girl will never hold a future job or gain financial independence. In a few years, when she meets her fate, her husband will control her finances. She doesn't know her rights, how to protect herself, or where to turn if she experiences harm. If she's ever a victim of a crime, she will not contact the police or set foot in a courtroom. She will move on quietly and avoid making eye contact with neighbors in order to escape the shame of being a victim. Now imagine that same girl encountering Coptic Orphans, an NGO ensuring that vulnerable children achieve their potential through education and one of the world's largest nonprofits operating in Egypt. Because of one intervention, this girl's trajectory changes. She's no longer thinking about her fate as a teenage wife and homemaker. Rather, she's making plans to study engineering and start a water purification project for her village. She finishes high school and earns her engineering degree. She learns not only reading and math, but also confidence, leadership, and how to recognize abuse and seek help through judicial institutions. Her mother is also involved, gaining independence and financial literacy. What began as support for the girl becomes a 2-generation intervention for a family eventually a community. Girls from her village start sharing her story and following her footsteps. This girl from Sharona is real. Her story is real. I had the pleasure of meeting her last year. She's just one of the tens of thousands of girls for whom Coptic Orphans has broken the cycle of injustice. When girls are surrounded by support through education, membership, family engagement, and community protection, they can exercise their rights and make informed decisions, access justice, participate in society, and dare to be at the forefront of decision-making processes. Coptic Orphans has conducted a valuable girl project for almost 25 years, and through this project, we have noticed that girls from various religious backgrounds have improved literacy rates by a staggering 90%. Additionally, girls and women initiated community projects benefiting nearly 800
I thank the distinguished representative of Coptic Orphans Support Association and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Australian Graduate Women.

Honorable Chair, Your Excellencies, distinguished guests, and civil society delegates, my name is Professor Jaya Dantas and I am from Australia. I speak on behalf of of Australian Graduate Women, Graduate Women International, and Curtin University. Australian Graduate Women places the highest priority on higher education of girls and women in the world. We believe that access to quality education and tertiary education advocates for women's rights, equality, and empowerment. We work with women graduates across all cultures, all fields of study, all professions, and all generations to empower women and girls through lifelong education for leadership, decision-making, and most importantly, peace. We view education as the catalyst to health and well-being, as essential for empowering women, reducing poverty, supporting human rights, and maintaining peace. To ensure that the Commission on the Status of Women effectively supports and addresses national legislative mechanisms for strengthening access to justice for all women and girls by equitable legal systems. We need to strengthen institutional capacity. We need to provide technical and financial assistance, enhance policy coordination, amplify grassroots engagement in many parts of the world, and secure sustainable funding. In 2026, Australia is centering its effort on balancing the scales of justice for women and girls through significant legislative reforms, increased funding, and increased advocacy. All of these initiatives target the persistent structural barriers against gender-based violence, financial stress, systemic inequality that prevents women from exercising their legal and regal rights. We have a National Access to Justice Partnership, a National Women's Justice Strategy, Family Law Act reforms, and specialist women's legal centers. Along with this, we have eliminated several discriminatory laws and practices. But global leadership and advocacy is needed to strengthen global norms and advance women's economic empowerment and leadership to address the structural barriers of violence and discrimination by implementing and enforcing laws to prevent gender-based violence. We can strengthen monitor and review and data collection appraisal and encourage real-time data monitoring through digital platforms to ensure transparency. we need collective action and continued advocacy. There's a powerful truth in achieving gender equality.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Australian Graduate Women and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of COC Netherlands.

Hello, my name is Nadia Swanson. My pronouns are they/them. I'm from the United States. And giving this intervention on behalf of the LBTI Caucus, a coalition of more than 200 organizations around the world. Across every region, lesbian, bisexual, transgender women, girls, gender nonconforming, and intersex people are facing escalating violence, discrimination, and systemic exclusion, including from accessing justice. These harms are the result of coordinated political attacks, discriminatory laws, and institutions that deny our communities access to justice, healthcare, housing, and safety. All leading medical and mental health organizations affirm how gender-affirming care is not only just safe, but prevents suicide, increases overall health outcomes, and all qualities of life. For many of the young people I work with globally, homelessness is not accidental. It is the predictable outcome of oppressive laws, family rejection, discrimination in schools, and the denial of gender-affirming care. Trans youth and young adults are often pushed into systems that criminalize their survival rather than protect their dignity and are left to fight for safe resources and support that are wildly underfunded and often far from home. These harms are not experienced equally. Black and brown and Indigenous trans women and girls face some of the highest levels of violence, poverty, and criminalization globally, shaped by the intersecting forces of racism, sexism, and transphobia. Transgender migrants and refugees face additional layers of risk, forced to flee persecution only to encounter detention, homelessness, and barriers to justice, healthcare, and legal recognition in the countries where they seek safety. And today we must speak clearly about what is happening in the United States. Experts have warned that the escalating targeted attacks of dehumanization, criminalization, and erasure targeting transgender people in the U.S. Reflects the early to middle stages of a genocidal process. These policies are not only about restricting rights, they aim to remove transgender people from public life entirely. Trans people in the US are being used as scapegoats to further authoritarian power and putting all people at risk of violence. When governments normalize anti-trans policies, those narratives travel across borders. We are already seeing the ripple effects: increased violence, emboldened anti-rights movements, and new laws targeting trans and intersex people globally. We all carry a responsibility to act now. But trans communities are not only thriving, we are building solutions. We know what works: safe and affordable housing, access to gender-affirming care, legal recognition, protection from violence, and meaningful inclusion decision-making. So today we call on the United Nations and member states to act, to reject any hostile amendments or proposals that would weaken the current text on gender equality commitments. Doing so would threaten the legitimacy of consensus-based agreements in future CSWs and other UN processes. States must ensure that commitments to gender equality apply to all women and girls, including—
I thank the distinguished representative of COC Netherlands and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Forum Mediterranea pour la Promotion des Droits du Citoyen.

Thank you, Madam Chair, ladies and gentlemen. As a defender of human rights and of civil society, our organization is committed to defending human rights and dignity and defending women that have been exposed to sexual violence following wars in particular. We are particularly concerned about thousands of women having been sexually exploited during wars and subject to sexual violence, which for them has caused a lot of physical and psychological damage that's lasting. Their suffering has never been recognized. Their rights to reparations have not been recognized either for these comfort women. And we suggest that that this issue of comfort women be recognized by UNESCO so that this tragedy will not be repeated. We must respect women's rights throughout the world. According to international criteria, human rights criteria, we reaffirm the following principles: the right to information, for example, Historic reality must be recognized and maintained and passed on to future generations, so that the importance of what happened to them is not diminished. And judicial authorities must prosecute those that commit these kinds of sexual crimes according to international law. They must also guarantee these. Survivors and their families significant reparations, including material reparations to enable them to recover their dignity and to ensure that they won't suffer from these kinds of crimes again. The survivors must live in dignity and be given health and psychological support and legal support in order to enable them to deal with the stigma. They also have the right to prevention. We need to strengthen human rights activities as well as ensure gender equality and punish and prevent sexual violence during conflicts. We would call upon the international community and all governments and educational institutions as well as the civil society to assume their historic responsibility towards this group and their survivors.
And now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Foundation for Studies and Research on Women.

I'm going to speak in Spanish. Gracias, señora presidenta. Thank you, Madam Chair. I've come here to speak on the Institute for the Study of Women and also NGOs for CSW and a lot of networks present here. For us in Latin America and the Caribbean, access to justice that began to be developed was lost. With the pandemic, and unfortunately, it didn't come back. Now, there are several reasons for this, but some of the reasons are linked to the lack of forward thinking in general in our legal systems when it comes to gender issues, and also because there's not very much interest in this, and that's the case in my country, Argentina, that has rejected and denied everything that has to do with women's rights because apparently we're equal. But as everybody knows, that's not the case. And in our region, unfortunately, what we're seeing is high levels of femicide. The worst form of violence suffered by women. And to that, we must add that we are champions in persecuting and murdering human rights defenders, and that's another one of the problems that affect us and where we haven't been able to overcome this. Violence continues to be something that affects us, particularly affecting girls. And that's bad enough, but what's worse is the impunity. We don't have security or the ability to apply a given method to contain obstetric violence and that's why we really are suffering now serious problems. The excuse that a lot of our countries give us is that they don't have enough money. That's just an excuse. The real thing is that there's been no political decision taken in order to improve access to justice for all kinds of violence. And in conclusion, let me say that in our region and in the world, I'd say, what we need is for there to be recognition of women's and girls' rights in all their diversity. Gender for us is a principle that was ratified in Beijing and we must—

the microphone has been cut off. Thank you very much. of the Foundation for Studies and Research on Women. Muchas gracias. And now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Latin American and Caribbean Women's Health Network.

A greeting from women from Latin America and the Caribbean. We demand a life free of violence. For women and for girls. This Commission has recognized that progress to bring about gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls to ensure they have full enjoyment of their rights, all of that has been put on hold. We do recognize that progress has been made, but there's a lot of backtracking that is standing in the way of us being autonomous and having a life free of violence because of of all these barriers that we see in access to justice, femicide, hate crimes, violence against political women figures, judges, human rights defenders. All of that sort of thing should stop right away. We need— we also have historical violence, child marriage, FGM, vicarious violence, obstetric violence, and today we are seeing digital violence as well in all forms and manifestations. And we don't see the law punishing this in very many countries. 80 years after the creation of the United Nations and 70 years following the creation of this Commission, we have to say that a lot of women are still seeing their most fundamental human rights being violated. This is why for all of this we're asking governments recognize the central nature of the right to development for women and girls, that equality must be assured by the implementation of international and national agreements already agreed to. We need to ensure the economic empowerment of women, guarantee their universal access to health and sexual and reproductive healthcare rights in accordance with the Program of Action on Population and Development and also the Beijing Platform of Action, which includes access to modern methods of contraception, information, comprehensive sexual education based on scientific evidence, and the inclusion of reproductive health in national strategies and programs recognizing that human rights include the right to have control over one's own sexuality and reproduction, which recognizes the importance of contributions that women's organizations can make. Our participation is not a privilege, it's a necessity in democracies, and to guarantee our funding is the duty of states. Of the Latin American and Caribbean Women's Health Network. And now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Imam Ali's Popular Students Relief Society.

Madam Chair, distinguished delegates, the International Association of Jewish Lawyers and Jurists was founded in 1968 by leading jurists of the 20th century with a clear mission: to mobilize the legal community in defense of human rights, the rule of law, and justice in international affairs. Today we work globally in courts, international institutions, and civil society to confront some of the most pressing legal challenges of our time, one of which is a persistent cycle of impunity surrounding the grave human— surrounding grave human rights violations, including conflict-related sexual violence. Sexual violence is tragically not new. For centuries, it has been used as instruments of warfare, often aimed at humiliating individuals and destroying communities. Yet today, recognition increases that such crimes are not incidental acts of brutality, but are frequently systematic tools of terror and control. As a Jewish legal organization, our engagement with this issue is also shaped by a deeper legal and historical perspective. Jewish legal tradition places extraordinary emphasis on the inherent dignity of every human being, or kavod ha-briyot, reflecting the same fundamental idea embedded in modern international humanitarian law that the right of belligerents to harm the enemy is not unlimited. Jewish history teaches another important lesson: silence and denial cannot— can be as dangerous as the crimes themselves. Too often atrocities are followed not only by silence but by reluctance to acknowledge uncomfortable facts. Credible evidence of sexual violence committed during the Hamas-led attacks of October 7th was, in some quarters, met with hesitation, doubt, or prolonged silence, including from organizations whose mandate is to defend women's rights. Victims are silenced a second time when CRSV is filtered through political considerations. Such double standards do not only harm the victims, they weaken the credibility of the global struggle against CRSV, Which, to effectively combat, this principle must be clear: sexual violence must be condemned, investigated, and prosecuted regardless of the identity of the perpetrators or victims. CRSV is not confronted to one conflict or region but is a global human rights challenge. While this discussion takes place within the CSW framework, this is not only a women's issue. Men and boys are also victims. Ultimately, this is about protecting the dignity of every human being. Breaking this cycle requires stronger international and domestic legal tools. It also requires cooperation between states, international institutions, and civil society. Thank you.

Yet for many women with disabilities, participation remains limited by barriers that persist in our institutions, in our policies, and in our attitudes. When we talk about inclusive decision-making, making, we must recognize the key enablers that make participation possible. Accessibility in all its forms is essential. It also means accessible information and communication and inclusive meeting formats to ensure that women with disabilities can engage equally in decisions discussions and decision-making processes. Non-discrimination must be guaranteed. Women with disabilities experience multiple intersecting forms of discrimination that continue to limit our voices in political, social, and economic spaces. Colleagues, meaningful participation is not only about being present here in this room. It is about being heard It is about being respected and being recognized as equal partners in shaping the policies that affect our lives as women with disabilities. In that regard, the participation of women with disabilities in high-level spaces such as CSW is really essential, necessary, and critical. It is also particularly relevant to this year's priority theme on access to justice. Too often, women with disabilities are perceived Only as mere recipients of protection. However, women with disabilities are also leaders and experts who are ready to contribute to inclusive justice systems. When women with disabilities participate fully and effectively, our institutions become more inclusive, our justice systems become more responsive, and our societies become stronger for everyone. We are here at the Commission to raise our voice for access to justice for women in all their diversity. Distinguished Chair, Excellencies, and colleagues, my name is Darin Khiyari. And I have the honor of speaking on behalf of the International Federation of Medical Students Associations, representing over 1.5 million medical, medical students from over 130 countries. Globally, nearly 1 in 3 women experience violence in their lifetime. However, many survivors do not report, not because it doesn't matter, but because of stigma, fear of retaliation, and mistrust in institutions. When justice is out of reach, survivors are left behind, and cycles of harm continue across generations. This underrepresentation matters because when women are excluded from policymaking spaces, the laws and the very systems that are meant to protect them fail to reflect their lived realities. Medical students, for example, are working in their communities to respond to gender-based violence, advocate for equitable health systems, and support the rights and well-being of women and girls. However, these efforts are often limited by a lack of access and decision-making spaces. Youth participation must move beyond consultation toward actual partnership. Therefore, the International Federation of Medical Students' Associations calls on member states to ensure legal frameworks are effectively implemented to protect women and girls from violence and discrimination, invest in accessible gender-responsive justice and health systems that provide comprehensive survival-centered care, ensure the meaningful participation of women and young people in decision-making at all levels, And finally, support civil society and youth-led organizations in advancing gender equity and human rights. Excellencies, medical students stand for health systems that are fair and for a world where every woman and girl can access justice, have a choice, and live free from violence. We can only achieve this with real commitment, accountability, and the political will to turn promises into change. I thank you. Thank you.

Thank you, Chair. I speak on behalf of the International Trade Union Confederations, which represent around 200 million workers all over the world. Global trade union movement welcomes the inclusion of decent work agenda in the agreed conclusion of CSW 70. This achievement stands in stark contrast to how the negotiations began, as in the draft document there was no mention at all to access to justice for women in the world of work. The text recommends fulfilling the obligations arising from relevant conventions of the International Labour Organization Addressing violence and harassment in the workplace, and tackling the gender pay gap. It also includes enforcing labour rights, including the rights to organize and collective bargaining, the transition from informal to formal and decent work, and right to redress and justice for victims of labour rights violations. Secondly, care economy. UN Member States commit to invest in the care economy, and strengthen care and support systems by recognizing, reducing, and redistributing women's disproportionate share of unpaid care and domestic work. Thirdly, trade unions are recognized as key promoters of access to justice for women. The ITUC and its affiliates will continue to hold governments to account to ensure these commitments are implemented and lead to tangible improvements in access to justice for women. In this sense, as trade unions, we call on member states to vote no on the US resolution that will be tabled on the 19th of March. CSW is where the world raises the bar on gender equality and not lowers it. Given the backlash against women's rights, human rights, and democracy across the globe, backlash that the trade union movement feels deeply, we call on the CSW to hold the line and continue to push forward. We need you. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the International Trade Union Confederation and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of IRIS Sustainable Development.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, as we advance the commitments of the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action, The rapid digitalization of legal systems raises a critical question: will artificial intelligence expand women's access to justice or entrench existing inequalities behind a veil of technological neutrality? AI is already shaping justice systems worldwide, from case management and legal research to risk assessment and decision support tools. When governed responsibly, AI can expand access to legal information, especially for women and girls facing geographic, financial, or social barriers. However, the risks are profound. AI systems are only as fair as the data and assumptions that shape them. Globally, over 2 billion women live under at least one discriminatory law, and justice data often reflects these structural biases. When trained on such data, AI systems can reinforce gender stereotypes, adversely affect marginalized women, and undermine due process. Opaque algorithms and weak oversight threaten women's rights to equality before the law, privacy, and effective remedies. Without strong safeguards, AI risks becoming a new systemic barrier since technology is never neutral. Ensuring access to justice for all women and girls in the digital age requires human rights-based and gender-responsive AI governance. This includes strengthening AI literacy across the legal sector while also empowering women as rights holders through accessible legal information and transparency whenever AI tools are used in legal decisions. In this context, concrete accountability mechanisms are critical. Commitments must be supported by gender and human rights impact assessments, transparency and explainability requirements, disaggregated data to detect bias, and enforceable remedies to challenge both human and automated decisions. To deliver on these commitments, we call on member states to establish and strengthen human rights-based governance for, for AI in justice systems, ensuring transparency, oversight, and safeguards against gender bias. Excellencies, access to justice is not defined by innovation alone. It depends on trust, accountability, and fairness. AI must dismantle discrimination, not encode it into digital systems. The choices we make today will determine whether AI narrows or deepens gender inequality. Ensuring justice for all women and girls in the age of AI is therefore not only a responsibility, it is a defining test of our collective commitment to gender equality. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Iris Sustainable Development and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Justicia Global.

Thank you, Madam Chair, distinguished delegates, and fellow civil society members. I address you today to raise urgent concerns about 2 issues: the torture and sexual abuse of Palestinian women in Israeli captivity and the total absence of justice for survivors. The prohibition of torture under the United Nations Convention Against Torture is absolute, yet myriad credible testimonies from Palestinian women detail pervasive acts of torture in Israeli prisons. These widespread, systematic, and brutal abuses constitute a de facto state policy and form part of the actus reus of genocide. As detailed by the UN Committee Against Torture in its November 2025 review of Israel. The following draws on hundreds of hours of digital evidence, testimonies, and reporting, as well as the experiences of 2 of my colleagues in Israeli prisons. In detention facilities including Stei Tayman detention camp, Hasharon Prison, and Ofer Prison, women reported filmed gang rapes, objects being inserted into their bodies, degrading and violent strip searches, beatings, and threats of blackmail using compromising photographs taken by guards. In Kitsiot Prison, 2 members of our team were detained, stripped naked, beaten, and threatened with death, while those detained with them were sexually assaulted. Despite the well-documented nature of these egregious violations, torture has been carried out with alarming impunity. According to documentation cited by the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel, of approximately 1,400 complaints of torture filed with the Israeli Ministry of Justice over the past 2 decades, zero indictments have been issued against alleged perpetrators. Only 3 cases resulted in a formal criminal investigation. Israel has also prevented independent monitoring, denying the International Committee of the Red Cross access to Palestinian detainees, in prisons and military detention. What is happening in Israel is clear: gender-based violence shielded by entrenched impunity. In the context of Israel's prolonged occupation and destruction of civic and civil society institutions in Palestine, Palestinian women have little to no access to justice for these abuses. We urge this Commission to take decisive action. to condemn the continued use of torture, to demand independent investigations, to ensure access for international monitors, to establish gender-sensitive safeguards, and to guarantee reparations from and accountability for all perpetrators. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Justicia Global and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Men Engaged Global Alliance.

Good evening, Madam Chair and distinguished guests. My name is Prita and I work with Breakthrough, which is a civil society organization based in India working to shift and address harmful gender norms. I represent MenEngage Global Alliance here in this forum as I deliver the oral statement. The current reality is stark. For 5.1 billion people, two-thirds of the world's population, meaningful justice is still out of reach, mostly women, girls, LGBTIQ people, and other marginalized communities. Across conflict zones, the bodies of women are not only collateral but battlegrounds. MenEngage Alliance, together with the members globally, have worked to advance gender equality by transforming the stereotypes around manhood and working with men and boys as agents of change to dismantle power inequalities. Without meaningful and accountable engagement of men and boys, it will be difficult to dismantle systemic injustices and ensure justice for all. We believe that justice cannot be realized while discriminatory norms and structures remain intact. It cannot flourish in systems designed without the voices and lived realities of those most affected by inequalities. Transforming justice systems requires those in positions of power to acknowledge institutional biases, reform discriminatory laws, and transform institutions from the inside out. At CSW 70, we urgently call on all member states to eliminate discriminatory laws and policies that restrict the fundamental rights and freedoms of all women, girls, LGBTIQ+ people, and marginalized communities. Without this commitment, gender equality remains a promise, not a reality. We also call on Member States to create opportunities and spaces for men in positions of power, like policymakers, judges, law enforcement, faith and traditional leaders, to critically reflect on their power and privilege and use them to advance women's leadership and strengthen gender-responsive justice systems. Finally, we emphasize the need for meaningful and active engagement of men and boys in dismantling patriarchal masculinities and advancing justice for all. This requires political will, resources, and courage. We urge member states to act with boldness and urgency. Justice delayed is justice denied. Thank you.
